name: Non-root vegetables (fruiting, brassica, bulb, stem and legume vegetables)
anchor: Per-produce-class sovereign maximum levels for lead and cadmium (EU Reg. 2023/915 and Switzerland VHK 817.022.15; Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2; AU-NZ Schedule 19; MERCOSUR GMC Res. 12/2011 and Paraguay Decreto 1335/2019; Israel MOH FCS-2016), nickel under EU Reg. 2024/1987, total and inorganic arsenic under MERCOSUR and Israel MOH FCS-2016, and total mercury under Hong Kong Cap. 132V and Israel MOH FCS-2016.
native_basis_label: fresh or frozen vegetable as sold, wet weight, edible portion after washing and separation of the edible part
scope_note: The residual fresh-vegetable row: every vegetable that is neither a root or tuber (its own row) nor a leaf vegetable or spinach (their own rows). It therefore covers fruiting vegetables (tomato, pepper, aubergine, okra and the cucurbits), head and flowering brassicas (cabbage heads, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi, Brussels sprouts), bulb vegetables (onion, shallot, garlic, leek), stalk and stem vegetables (celery, asparagus, fennel, rhubarb, globe artichoke) and fresh legume vegetables (green beans, garden peas, mangetout, fresh edamame in pod). Frozen forms share the fresh wet-weight basis. OUT OF SCOPE: dried pulses and their products (Category 27); sweet corn, which the Swiss and EU fruiting-vegetable lead rows expressly exclude and which routes with cereals to Category 3; edible fungi (Category 29); leafy brassicas such as kale, pak choi and collards (leafy-vegetables-other row, matching the Hong Kong and Swiss leafy-versus-head brassica split); pickled, fermented and brined forms (pickled-fermented-vegetables row); canned vegetables in tinplate (Category 7); vegetable juices (Category 5); products marketed for ages 0 to 5 (Category 1). COLLAPSED SOVEREIGN SPLITS, THE LARGEST IN THIS CATEGORY: every credible instrument subdivides this row, and the subdivisions differ by up to sixfold. For lead, Hong Kong, Switzerland and Israel set 50 ug/kg for fruiting vegetables against 100 ug/kg for bulb, brassica, stem and legume vegetables, and AU-NZ sets 300 ug/kg for brassicas. For cadmium, Switzerland sets 20 ug/kg for fruiting and legume vegetables, 30 ug/kg for bulb and stem vegetables and 40 ug/kg for head and flowering brassicas, while Hong Kong sets 100 ug/kg for legume, stalk and stem vegetables. For total arsenic, MERCOSUR sets 100 ug/kg for bulb, cucurbit, other fruiting and leguminous vegetables and 300 ug/kg for brassicas. For nickel, EU Reg. 2024/1987 sets 400 ug/kg for fruiting vegetables, 500 ug/kg for brassicas, 900 ug/kg for bulb vegetables and 1000 ug/kg for legume vegetables. The row binds the strictest applicable value in each cell, so onions, broccoli and green beans certify against fruiting-vegetable values that no government applies to them. This is the row whose taxonomy split is most worth making.
basis_guard: wet weight|portion ordinarily consumed|as listed|product as offered to consumer|product as placed on market|as sold|as_sold|as consumed|commodity|edible part
basis_guard_note: Every named anchor for this row must sit in a dietary as-sold, wet-weight, edible-part or portion-ordinarily-consumed basis. The guard rejects the register's article and material bases (toy and food-contact migration, textile and leather extraction, fertiliser and growing-media dry matter, colour-additive ingredient specifications, animal-feed 12 percent moisture), any one of which would be a basis conflation if it anchored a food row.
method: HMTc Method v2.0 (government-limit-only; the strictest applicable sovereign maximum level for the row's product form in the row's native basis, a disclosed read-across where the exact cell is unregulated, a substantiated not-material determination, or a control; never occurrence-derived)

Pb.basis: wet weight, fresh vegetable as sold
Pb.label: Three independent credible regulators set lead at 50 ug/kg for fruiting vegetables (Switzerland VHK Fruchtgemüse, Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 9 for both cucurbit and non-cucurbit fruiting vegetables, Israel MOH FCS-2016 category 3.4 for tomato, cucumber and pepper); the bulb, brassica, stem and legume rows of the same instruments sit at 100 ug/kg and the AU-NZ and MERCOSUR brassica rows at 300 ug/kg.
Pb.substantiation: The 50 ug/kg value is a direct maximum level for the fruiting vegetables that are the largest members of this row by volume, and it is the strictest value applicable to any member. It is selected because one published HMTc value must hold across the whole row and a value of 100 ug/kg would certify tomato and cucumber lots that are unlawful in Hong Kong, Switzerland and Israel. The full candidate set is named so the collapsed splits are visible in the derivation report; the recommended taxonomy fix is to split fruiting from bulb, brassica, stem and legume vegetables.

Cd.basis: wet weight, fresh vegetable as sold
Cd.label: Switzerland VHK 817.022.15 sets cadmium at 20 ug/kg for fruiting vegetables (excluding aubergines) and for legume vegetables, the strictest sovereign cadmium maximum level applicable to any member of this row; the Swiss stem and bulb rows sit at 30 ug/kg, the Swiss head and flowering brassica row at 40 ug/kg, and the Hong Kong, MERCOSUR, Paraguayan and Israeli rows at 50 to 100 ug/kg.
Cd.substantiation: The Swiss annex mirrors EU Reg. 2023/915, whose per-class cadmium rows are absent from the register's EU coverage, and 20 ug/kg is a direct maximum level for the fruiting and legume vegetables that dominate this row. The named set discloses the full five-step government split (20, 30, 40, 50, 100 ug/kg) that this taxonomy row collapses; onions, celery, cabbage heads and broccoli are consequently held to a value one and a half to five times stricter than their own sovereign class value.

tAs.basis: wet weight, fresh vegetable as sold
tAs.label: MERCOSUR GMC Res. 12/2011 and Paraguay Decreto 1335/2019 set total arsenic at 100 ug/kg for bulb, cucurbit, other fruiting and leguminous vegetables, against 300 ug/kg for brassicas; Hong Kong sets 500 ug/kg for vegetables and Israel 1000 ug/kg.
tAs.substantiation: Direct maximum levels for four of the five sub-classes in this row. The brassica carve-out at 300 ug/kg is named so the collapsed split is visible; head and flowering brassicas are held to the stricter 100 ug/kg value.

iAs.label: Israel MOH FCS-2016 category 3 sets the only inorganic-arsenic maximum level any credible government writes for fruits and vegetables (60 ug/kg); the EU, Codex, FDA, AU-NZ, Hong Kong and Swiss instruments set inorganic-arsenic maximum levels only for rice, juices, seaweed and infant food.
iAs.substantiation: Inorganic arsenic is the health-relevant arsenic species and is never satisfied by the total-arsenic cell; both are reported. This value is a direct maximum level for the product class, not a read-across, and it sits well below the total-arsenic ceiling for the same row, so the species cell is the binding arsenic constraint in practice.

tHg.basis: food as listed in Cap 132V Part 2 Schedule; source unit mg/kg
tHg.label: Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 12 sets total mercury for vegetables other than edible fungi at 10 ug/kg, the strictest sovereign total-mercury maximum level applicable to this product form; Israel MOH FCS-2016 category 3 sets 30 ug/kg for the same commodity class.
tHg.substantiation: Both named rows are direct maximum levels for the vegetable class in an as-sold basis. Hong Kong binds. Edible fungi are expressly outside the Hong Kong row (they carry 100 ug/kg under the same item) and route to Category 29, so the 10 ug/kg value is not being borrowed from a mushroom limit.

MeHg.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets a methylmercury maximum level for this product form: asensio2023-madrid-mushrooms-mercury measured methylmercury in this matrix, so the species is not absent and no not-material determination is supportable. Methylmercury is therefore held under mandatory analytical control rather than recorded not-material, and it remains bounded by identity below the published total-mercury ceiling for this row (methylmercury cannot exceed total mercury). No methylmercury ceiling is invented.
MeHg.reference_method: Methylmercury by GC-ICP-MS or EN 16801, required only on a lot whose total mercury reaches 60 percent of the published total-mercury ceiling; any quantifiable methylmercury on such a lot is investigated and the lot is held pending root-cause analysis.

Ni.basis: wet weight, fresh vegetable as sold
Ni.label: EU Reg. 2024/1987 sets nickel at 400 ug/kg for fruiting vegetables, mirrored by Switzerland VHK Fruchtgemüse and Stängelgemüse; the same instruments set 500 ug/kg for brassicas, 900 ug/kg for bulb vegetables and 1000 ug/kg for legume vegetables except soy beans and edamame.
Ni.substantiation: Direct maximum levels from the only comprehensive dietary nickel instrument in existence, named across all four sub-classes so the collapsed split is visible. Soy beans and edamame carry a separate 6000 ug/kg nickel row; fresh edamame in pod stays in this row and is therefore held to 400 ug/kg, fifteen times stricter than its own sovereign class, which is recorded as an outstanding taxonomy item. Dry beans, lupins and pulses route to Category 27. AUDIT DISPOSITION AND REGISTER DEFECT: the scan surfaces ch_vhk_2026_ni_kohlgemuse_100 at 100 ug/kg as stricter and unselected. It is not adopted because it is a defective register row: its own note reads 'fluessig' (liquid) and its sibling ch_vhk_2026_ni_kohlgemuse_400 reads 'in Pulverform, nur aus Sojaproteinisolaten oder gemischt' (powder form, from soy protein isolates or mixed), which are the EU Reg. 2024/1987 infant and young-child formula nickel maximum levels of 100 (liquid) and 400 (soy-isolate powder) mis-assigned to the Swiss brassica scope during ingest. Three register rows carry the identical product_scope string 'Kohlgemuese' at 100, 400 and 500 ug/kg; only the 500 ug/kg row carries the genuine brassica note ('bezogen auf Frischgewicht', on fresh weight) and matches the EU brassica value it mirrors, and that is the row named here. The two defective rows are reported for register correction rather than silently used or silently ignored.

Sn.rationale: Every tin maximum level in the register is scoped to canned product: EU Reg. 2023/915 sets 200000 ug/kg for canned foods and 100000 ug/kg for canned beverages, Codex CXS 193-1995 and AU-NZ Schedule 19 set 250000 ug/kg for canned foods, and Hong Kong Cap. 132V sets 250000 ug/kg for canned food other than canned beverages. Those limits regulate one contamination pathway, dissolution of tin from tinplate into the packed food. This row is not packed in tinplate, so the pathway that every sovereign tin limit addresses is physically absent and any tin present is dietary background rather than packaging migration. Fresh and frozen vegetables in this row are sold loose, bagged, netted or in polymer trays. Hermetically sealed tinplate presentations of this commodity route to the canned-foods row in Category 7 and carry the canned-foods tin maximum level there.
Sn.reference_method: Total tin by ICP-MS on every lot as part of the mandatory eight-totals panel; a result above 50 ug/kg is investigated for a metal-contact source in harvest, wash, transport or packing before the lot is released.
Sn.regulatory_basis: No jurisdiction sets a tin maximum level for non-canned produce; all tin maximum levels in the register are conditioned on a canned (tinplate) presentation, and the EU rows expressly exclude canned dried and canned powdered products from even that scope.
Sn.jurisdictions_checked: EU Reg. 2023/915; EU Reg. 2024/1987 (nickel); Switzerland VHK 817.022.15 (2026 metal/metalloid annex); Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2 Schedule; AU-NZ Food Standards Code Schedule 19; MERCOSUR GMC Res. 12/2011 and Paraguay Decreto 1335/2019; Israel MOH FCS-2016; Codex CXS 193-1995; US FDA (21 CFR, action levels)

Al.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets an aluminium contaminant maximum level for any fruit, vegetable or produce form in any jurisdiction. The register's aluminium limits are drinking-water and bottled-water parameters, infant-formula maximum levels, a food-contact plastics specific migration limit, toy migration limits, and permitted-additive levels for baked and starch foods; none of them regulates aluminium as a contaminant of produce. Aluminium is also the third most abundant element in the earth's crust and appears in produce largely as soil-derived and root-associated mineral content rather than as process contamination, so no near-neighbour read-across is supportable either. Under the government-limit-only method HMTc publishes no standalone aluminium number for this row.
Al.reference_method: Total aluminium by ICP-MS on every lot, reported to the applicant. Document any aluminium-containing processing aid, packaging contact or anti-caking agent, comply with the additive rules of every market of sale, and investigate any result that is an outlier against the applicant's own lot history.

Cr.screen_note: Total chromium is recorded as a SCREEN, not a protective ceiling. Dietary chromium is dominated by nutritionally essential Cr(III); the health-relevant species is Cr(VI), which is controlled separately by reflex speciation. A lot may satisfy this screen and still fail on Cr(VI), and the screen is excluded from the firm-limit count.
Cr.basis: food as listed in Cap 132V Part 2 Schedule; source unit mg/kg
Cr.label: Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 7 sets total chromium for vegetables other than pulses at 500 ug/kg, the only dietary total-chromium maximum level any credible government writes for this product form.
Cr.substantiation: Named as the sovereign total-chromium value for the vegetable class in its as-sold basis. Pulses are expressly outside this row (1000 ug/kg under the same item) and route to Category 27. Total chromium never satisfies the Cr(VI) cell.

Cr-VI.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum level for any food in any jurisdiction; every Cr(VI) limit in the register governs articles and materials (toys, textiles, leather, fertilisers, electrical equipment), not diet. Chromium in produce is dominated by nutritionally essential Cr(III), and Cr(VI) is not stable in the plant matrix: fruit and vegetable tissue is an aqueous, organic-acid and ascorbate-rich reducing medium in which Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III), so a reported Cr(VI) value in this matrix reflects extraction conditions rather than the chromium species the consumer ingests. Hexavalent chromium is therefore bounded by the published total-chromium screen for this row (Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 7, 500 ug/kg) and controlled by reflex speciation rather than by a published number.
Cr-VI.reference_method: Total chromium by ICP-MS on every lot. Any total-chromium result at or above 100 ug/kg triggers Cr(VI) speciation by EN 15192 or EPA 6800 IC-ICP-MS isotope dilution; any quantifiable Cr(VI) at LOQ fails the lot. Cr(VI) is never published as a panel number.
Cr-VI.regulatory_basis: No jurisdiction sets a dietary Cr(VI) maximum level; the register's Cr(VI) rows are article and material limits (EU 2009/48 toys, EU 2018/1513 textiles, EU 301/2014 leather, EU 2019/1009 fertilisers, EU RoHS). The total-chromium parent for this row is published.
Cr-VI.jurisdictions_checked: EU Reg. 2023/915; EU Reg. 2024/1987 (nickel); Switzerland VHK 817.022.15 (2026 metal/metalloid annex); Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2 Schedule; AU-NZ Food Standards Code Schedule 19; MERCOSUR GMC Res. 12/2011 and Paraguay Decreto 1335/2019; Israel MOH FCS-2016; Codex CXS 193-1995; US FDA (21 CFR, action levels)
